checks.title: Scope
checks.detail: Set the time window to catch the incident.

checks.title: Evidence
checks.detail: Opened one matching event to confirm it was real.

answer.evidence: The KQL result and expanded event connect ${var.finding_phrase} to ${truth.scope}.

goals.title: Set the time window
goals.concept: Setting a time range separates the incident from everyday, background activity.
goals.narration: Set the shortest practical time window that still includes when the incident was first noticed.
goals.reasoning: A tight time range keeps the incident in view without letting older, unrelated data throw off the comparison.
goals.evidence: The histogram and results should refresh to the window you picked.

demonstration.narration:
Set the time picker at the top to the last ${var.window_spelled}.

The report says this incident was first noticed ${detected_offset_minutes} minutes ago, so this is the shortest practical range, in five-minute steps, that still reaches that moment instead of pulling in a much longer history.
demonstration.reasoning:
We derive the range from the report's one firm timing fact: the incident was noticed ${detected_offset_minutes} minutes ago.

Rounding that age up to a practical five-minute boundary keeps the report and the picker consistent, gives us the records for ${truth.scope} since the first notice, and avoids comparing them with unnecessary older traffic before we look for ${var.finding_phrase}.
demonstration.evidence:
Once the range is set, the histogram and result count refresh to the last ${var.window_spelled}.

We haven't proved a cause yet — we've only chosen a range that reaches the reported incident without an oversized window, so the next search over ${truth.scope} has useful context.

hints: Start with when the problem was first noticed: ${detected_offset_minutes} minutes ago.
Use the date picker at the top of Discover (or click and drag on the date histogram); choose a short range that still reaches the reported time. For a live view you can also turn on auto-refresh.
Set the range to the last ${var.window_spelled}; Show me can do it for you.

goals.title: Isolate the decisive records
goals.concept: A query should narrow the evidence without assuming more than the brief establishes.
goals.narration: Use KQL to isolate the field pattern that answers the operational question.
goals.reasoning: Filtering the decisive field makes the abnormal group comparable with normal records.
goals.evidence: The remaining result set contains the scenario signal.

demonstration.narration:
The window from the last step still contains normal, healthy traffic, so enter this KQL query in the search bar: ${var.query}.

It uses ${var.field} to narrow this run to the records most likely to reveal ${var.finding_phrase}.
demonstration.reasoning:
The scoped window still contains normal and background events.

Filtering on ${var.field} removes that noise and tests whether evidence for ${var.finding_phrase} is actually present in ${truth.scope}, instead of assuming the brief is correct.
demonstration.evidence:
When the query runs, the table should shrink to the scenario signal.

Look for ${var.field} values and neighbouring fields that point to ${var.finding_phrase}; that result supports, but does not yet fully corroborate, “${truth.conclusion}”

hints: Identify the field that separates the abnormal records.

Use the KQL bar — combine clauses with and/or/not and parentheses, match with * wildcards or test a field with field:* — or Add filter (field, operator, value) and filter for or out (is not) a value from a row or a field's top values.
Filter on ${var.field}; Show me can enter a reference query.

goals.title: Check the evidence in one event
goals.concept: A conclusion is stronger when you open one typical event and check it.
goals.narration: Open one typical result and read the fields that back up the finding.
goals.reasoning: Checking a single event stops you from drawing a conclusion from totals alone.
goals.evidence: The event you open contains the facts that back up the finding.

demonstration.narration:
Expand the first filtered result and read its fields one by one.

We expect one real event to connect ${var.finding_phrase} with ${truth.scope}, rather than asking you to trust just the histogram or the result count.
demonstration.reasoning:
A total can look convincing even when it's made up of the wrong kind of event or an unrelated record.

Opening one typical event checks that the key values really do appear together in the same event and back up the filtered signal.
demonstration.evidence:
The event you opened is the evidence that backs it up.

If its fields match ${var.finding_phrase} and ${truth.scope}, then the signal and the event together support the conclusion: ${truth.conclusion}

hints: Check one typical record instead of relying only on the count.
Expand a row, open a field's top values, or change the table — add the key field as a column, or hide one you don't need.
Open the first result; Show me can do it for you.

goals.title: Submit a conclusion you can back up
goals.concept: A good answer states the finding, its scope, and the evidence that links them.
goals.narration: Write down the conclusion and point to the evidence for it.
goals.reasoning: The answer should keep what you saw separate from what you worked out.
goals.evidence: The answer points to the signal and the event that backs it up.
hints: Sum up what the evidence shows.
Use the coach's answer form and include your evidence references.
Submit the finding, scope, conclusion, and evidence; Show me shows the reference summary.
